articles.title: The Letter That Said You Owe Nothing
articles.dek: Two former debt collectors found a way to erase debts people had been paying on for years. Hebrews 9 describes a bigger payment, made once, that reaches the place no annual offering could touch.
articles.quote: Christ paid the whole debt once, so the energy you once spent on guilt can now be spent on love.
articles.body:
In 2014, two men who had spent years in the debt collection business sat down with an unusual idea. Craig Antico and Jerry Ashton knew the trade from the inside. They knew that when a hospital bill goes unpaid long enough, the debt is often bundled with thousands of others and sold to collectors for a tiny fraction of its face value, sometimes a penny on the dollar or less. The collector who buys it then spends years pursuing the full amount from people who are often still sick, often behind on rent, and frightened every time the phone rings.

Antico and Ashton asked a question nobody in their industry had any reason to ask. If a bundle of debt could be bought that cheaply, what would happen if someone bought it and simply erased it? They founded a nonprofit called RIP Medical Debt (known today as Undue Medical Debt), gathered donations, and began purchasing medical debt on the same market the collectors used. Then, instead of calling the debtors, they mailed each one a letter saying the balance was gone, with nothing to sign and nothing to repay.

Over the following years the organization has wiped away billions of dollars of medical debt for millions of families. The responses that came back to the office were deeply human. People wrote about years of dreading the mailbox, about small monthly payments that never seemed to bring the total down, and about standing in the driveway in tears over a single sheet of paper. One payment, made once by strangers they would never meet, accomplished what years of their own payments could not.

Filipinos understand that weight well. Anyone who has borrowed from a five-six lender knows the feeling of paying every week and somehow owing just as much, and the sound of the collector's motorcycle stopping outside the gate. Each payment proves you are trying, and each payment also reminds you that you are still in debt. The ninth chapter of Hebrews describes a whole system of worship that carried something like that weight, and then it tells us about the payment that ended it.

Hebrews was written to Jewish believers in Jesus who were under pressure and tempted to drift back to the old forms of worship they had grown up with. The writer, whose name we do not know, answers them by walking slowly through the tabernacle, the great tent where Israel worshiped during its years in the wilderness. In the first room, the Holy Place, stood the lampstand and the table with its consecrated bread (Hebrews 9:2). Behind a second curtain lay the Most Holy Place, holding the ark of the covenant, its gold-covered chest guarding the stone tablets, with the cherubim of the Glory spreading their wings over the atonement cover (Hebrews 9:3–5).

Picture the one day each year when that inner room was entered. On the Day of Atonement, described in Leviticus 16, the high priest bathed, set aside his splendid robes, and dressed in plain linen. He carried burning incense behind the curtain so that a cloud would cover the atonement cover, and then he returned with the blood of a bull and a goat and sprinkled it there, first for his own sins and then for the nation's. Outside, the crowd waited in silence. Later Jewish tradition, preserved in the Mishnah, remembers that the high priest kept his prayer inside short so that the waiting people would not grow afraid he had died in the presence of God.

Hebrews sums up that tense and holy day in one sentence: “But only the high priest entered the inner room, and that only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance” (Hebrews 9:7). The writer then points out that the very design carried a message. The closed curtain showed “that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed” (Hebrews 9:8), and the offerings “were not able to clear the conscience of the worshiper” (Hebrews 9:9). The next year the priest would have to do it all again, and the year after that. Hebrews later calls those sacrifices “an annual reminder of sins” (Hebrews 10:3), which sounds very much like a weekly payment to the five-six man.

Then the chapter turns. Christ came as high priest, and he entered a sanctuary “not made with human hands” (Hebrews 9:11). “He did not enter by means of the blood of goats and calves; but he entered the Most Holy Place once for all by his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). The writer finishes with an argument his Jewish readers would have recognized, reasoning from the lesser to the greater:

“The blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that they are outwardly clean. How much more, then, will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our consciences from acts that lead to death, so that we may serve the living God!” (Hebrews 9:13–14)

The Greek word for conscience here is syneidēsis, which literally means a “knowing-with.” It is the inner witness that sits with you at night and remembers what you did. The old sacrifices could make a worshiper ceremonially clean on the outside, fit to enter the courts again, but they could not reach that inner witness. The deepest debt we carry is lodged exactly there, and Hebrews says Christ's offering goes all the way in.

The word redemption in verse 12 also deserves attention. In Greek it is lytrōsis, a word from the ancient marketplace for the price paid to release a captive or settle what someone owed. Paul uses the same picture when he says God “canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14). The phrase “once for all” translates ephapax, a word that closes the account permanently. One way to read Hebrews 9, then, is as the moment the whole bundle of our debt was purchased by someone who had no intention of collecting it.

The most surprising part of the verse comes at the very end. Christ cleanses our consciences “so that we may serve the living God.” The verb for serve is latreuō, the same word used for priestly worship in the tabernacle, and the same root behind “the worshiper” in verse 9. The people who once stood outside the curtain waiting are now invited to do the work of priests. The cleansing has a purpose, and the purpose is a life of service to a God who is alive.

The families who received those letters often described what came next. Money that had gone to old bills could now buy medicine, school supplies, or a bag of rice. Sleep returned, and so did the courage to answer the phone. In the same way, a conscience set free from guilt releases enormous energy that was being spent on regret, self-punishment, and anxious religious effort. Hebrews calls those efforts “acts that lead to death,” and they can include sincere attempts to earn back God's favor through extra prayers, extra service, or extra misery.

Many believers are still making payments on a debt Christ has already settled. They replay an old failure every time they kneel, or they quietly assume God is still waiting for one more installment before he fully accepts them. If that describes you, consider taking a few minutes today to name the thing you keep paying on, read Hebrews 9:12 aloud over it, and thank God that the account is closed. Then take the energy that guilt has been consuming and give it to someone else, perhaps through a visit, a phone call, or a gift to a neighbor who is carrying a burden of their own.

Christ paid the whole debt once, so the energy you once spent on guilt can now be spent on love. The curtain is open, the High Priest has come out of the sanctuary alive, and the letter with your name on it has already been sent. You are free to open it, believe what it says, and spend this Monday serving the living God with a clean heart.

articles.title: Seven Days Without a Sermon
articles.dek: Ezekiel had just seen the glory of God and swallowed a scroll full of hard words. Then he walked into the refugee camp and, for a whole week, said nothing at all.
articles.quote: The right to speak into someone's pain is usually earned on the floor beside them.
articles.body:
In May 1997, Fred Rogers walked onto the stage at the Daytime Emmy Awards to receive a lifetime achievement award. The auditorium was full of television people, men and women who measure their worth in seconds of airtime, and Rogers, then nearly seventy, asked them for something their industry almost never allows. He asked for silence. "All of us have special ones who have loved us into being," he said. "Would you just take, along with me, ten seconds to think of the people who have helped you to become who you are, those who have cared about you and wanted what was best for you in life. Ten seconds of time. I'll watch the time."

Then he lifted his wrist and actually watched it. The cameras kept rolling while a room of polished celebrities sat in the quiet with their own memories, and within moments people were wiping their eyes. Nearly thirty years later, that pause is still the part of the evening people share with one another. Rogers was an ordained Presbyterian minister, and he understood something a young priest named Ezekiel learned on a canal bank in Babylon twenty-six centuries earlier: there are seasons when the most faithful thing a messenger of God can do is sit quietly among people for a while.

Ezekiel's story begins in 593 BC, in what he calls "the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin" (Ezekiel 1:2). Four years earlier the Babylonian army had emptied Jerusalem of its leading citizens, its craftsmen and its priests, and marched them hundreds of miles east (2 Kings 24:14). Ezekiel was among them. He opens his book with a strangely personal detail: "In my thirtieth year... while I was among the exiles by the Kebar River, the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God" (Ezekiel 1:1). Thirty was the age at which a priest began his service at the temple (Numbers 4:3). This should have been the year Ezekiel finally stood at the altar in Jerusalem, and instead he was living beside an irrigation canal in a foreign land, a priest with no temple at all.

Then the sky tore open. A storm rolled in from the north, flashing with fire, and out of it came four living creatures with wings and faces, and wheels "full of eyes all around" that moved in every direction at once (Ezekiel 1:18). Above them stretched a sparkling expanse, and above that a throne, and on the throne a figure blazing like fire, wrapped in a radiance "like the appearance of a rainbow in the clouds on a rainy day" (Ezekiel 1:28). The glory of the LORD, which every Israelite believed lived in the temple in Jerusalem, had come to Babylon on wheels. Ezekiel did the only sensible thing and fell on his face.

God lifted him up and gave him a commission no one would envy. He was being sent to a people who were "obstinate and stubborn" (Ezekiel 2:4), and he was told plainly, "Do not be afraid, though briers and thorns are all around you and you live among scorpions" (Ezekiel 2:6). A hand reached out holding a scroll written on both sides with "words of lament and mourning and woe" (Ezekiel 2:10), and God told him to eat it. He did, and to his surprise "it tasted as sweet as honey in my mouth" (Ezekiel 3:3). Yet when the Spirit carried him away, he went "in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit, with the strong hand of the LORD on me" (Ezekiel 3:14). The word of God was sweet to him, and the task of carrying it to wounded people was heavy. Anyone who has ever had to deliver hard news to someone they love knows both of those feelings at the same time.

By every expectation, the next verse should show Ezekiel marching into the camp, scroll in his belly and fire in his bones, preaching at full volume. Here is what he actually writes:

"I came to the exiles who lived at Tel Aviv near the Kebar River. And there, where they were living, I sat among them for seven days, deeply distressed." (Ezekiel 3:15)

The man who had just seen the throne of heaven spent his first week among the exiles saying nothing. The older King James Version renders the verse in a way many readers have never forgotten: "I sat where they sat." He sat on their ground, in their settlement, at the level of their grief. The place name adds its own ache. Tel Aviv likely comes from the Akkadian til abubi, "mound of the flood," a name for an old ruin heap that people imagined had been left by the great deluge. God's people were literally camping on a pile of rubble, and Ezekiel took his seat in it beside them. (The modern Israeli city borrowed its name from this very verse, which gives it a quietly hopeful afterlife.)

The phrase "deeply distressed" translates the Hebrew word mashmim, from a root, shamem, that means to be stunned, appalled, or made desolate. The prophets use the same root to describe a land that has been emptied and ruined. One way to read Ezekiel's week, then, is that he let his people's desolation come into him before he ever put it into words. He had eaten a scroll of lament, and now he was learning what lament looks like on actual faces.

Seven days also carried weight in Israel's memory. It was the traditional length of mourning: Joseph mourned his father Jacob for seven days (Genesis 50:10), and Job's friends "sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was" (Job 2:13). Many readers agree that those silent days were the wisest thing Job's friends ever did, and the trouble started only when they opened their mouths. There is one more echo worth holding gently. A priest's ordination in Israel lasted seven days (Leviticus 8:33). Ezekiel, in his thirtieth year, was denied his ordination at the temple altar, and this suggests God gave him a different one: a seven-day consecration on the dusty ground of a refugee camp, set apart for ministry by sitting with grieving people. Only "at the end of seven days" did the word of the LORD come to him again (Ezekiel 3:16).

Most of us are quick to speak when someone we love is hurting. A friend tells us about the diagnosis, a cousin's marriage is falling apart, a coworker's son has stopped coming home, and we reach at once for the right verse, the practical fix, or the story of how we went through something similar. Our intentions are good, and sometimes those words help. Yet Ezekiel's week reminds us that the right to speak into someone's pain is usually earned on the floor beside them. People rarely remember the advice they received in their darkest week, but they remember for the rest of their lives who came and stayed.

Filipinos already know this wisdom in their bones. At a lamay, the wake that often runs for several nights, relatives and neighbors come after work, drink coffee, share a little food, and simply keep the family company until the small hours. Few of them give speeches, and the family is comforted all the same. The presence itself is the message: you are not alone on this mound of rubble. Ezekiel's ministry to a nation began with that same posture, and his later words of judgment and of hope carried the authority of a man who had first sat where they sat.

If someone in your life is carrying a heavy week right now, you might visit them, or call, and resolve before you arrive to ask one honest question and then listen without trying to repair anything. Let there be silence if silence comes, even ten seconds of it, and trust that God is working in the quiet. And if you are the one sitting in the rubble today, take heart from the opening scene of this book. The glory of God traveled all the way to a canal in Babylon to find a displaced priest on his thirtieth birthday, and then God sent that priest to sit with the rest of the exiles. The same God has not lost track of where you are living, and he is very good at sending someone to sit beside you.

articles.title: A Heart That Can Still Feel
articles.dek: A surgeon in India found that pain was quietly protecting his patients. Centuries earlier, a psalmist had found the same mercy in his own hard season.
articles.quote: The ache you carry today may be the very nerve that keeps your heart tender toward God.
articles.body:
In the late 1940s, a young English surgeon named Paul Brand began working at the Christian Medical College in Vellore, in southern India. He was drawn to patients most doctors preferred to avoid: men and women with leprosy, whose fingers and toes slowly shortened and disappeared over the years. Nearly everyone at the time assumed the disease itself ate away the flesh. Brand was not so sure. He watched his patients closely, and he began to notice something strange about the way they used their hands.

One day he struggled to turn a rusty key in a stubborn padlock, and a boy in the ward offered to help. The boy twisted it open with ease. Only afterward did Brand see that the key had cut the boy's finger to the bone, and the boy had felt nothing at all. Slowly the pieces came together. The bacteria that cause leprosy, Brand concluded, attack the nerve endings first. Once those nerves fall silent, the body loses its warning system. A patient grips a hot cooking pot, walks for miles on a blistered foot, or sleeps while rats nibble at a finger, and never knows until the harm is done. The flesh was being lost to ordinary days that had stopped hurting.

That discovery changed the treatment of leprosy around the world, through protective shoes, careful hand training, and the simple habit of inspecting the body every evening. It also changed how Brand spoke about suffering for the rest of his life. He liked to say, in one form or another, that he thanked God for inventing pain, because pain is the faithful messenger that keeps a body whole. Filipinos who know the long story of Culion in Palawan, once home to one of the largest leprosy colonies in the world, can sense how much mercy was hidden in that small insight.

A writer long ago reached the same conclusion about the soul. He left it in Psalm 119, the longest chapter in the Bible, a careful poem of twenty-two stanzas. Each stanza has eight lines, and every line in a stanza begins with the same letter of the Hebrew alphabet, moving from first letter to last like a child reciting the ABCs. We do not know the poet's name. We do know he was under pressure. Earlier he writes, "Though rulers sit together and slander me, your servant will meditate on your decrees" (Psalm 119:23), and in today's stanza he says, "Though the arrogant have smeared me with lies, I keep your precepts with all my heart" (Psalm 119:69). This is a man who has been talked about, misjudged, and worn down.

Today's stanza, verses 65 to 72, belongs to the Hebrew letter teth. Very few Hebrew words begin with that letter, and the poet seems to have welcomed the limitation, because one of them is tov, the ordinary Hebrew word for "good." He returns to it again and again. "Do good to your servant according to your word, LORD" (Psalm 119:65). "Teach me knowledge and good judgment" (Psalm 119:66). "You are good, and what you do is good" (Psalm 119:68). Even the stanza's final line opens with tov li, "good to me," which the NIV renders "The law from your mouth is more precious to me than thousands of pieces of silver and gold" (Psalm 119:72). Line after line, the man who has been smeared with lies keeps circling back to the goodness of God. Then he says the most surprising thing in the whole stanza.

"It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees." (Psalm 119:71)

He has already confessed the background in verse 67: "Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I obey your word." The word for "afflicted" comes from the Hebrew root anah, which means to be bowed down or pressed low. It is the same root Moses used when he reminded Israel of their forty years in the desert: "He humbled you, causing you to hunger and then feeding you with manna, which neither you nor your ancestors had known, to teach you that man does not live on bread alone but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 8:3). The psalmist seems to be living a small version of that wilderness story. He was pressed low, and in the pressing he discovered a hunger for "the law from your mouth," the very phrase Moses had used about where true bread comes from.

The verse just before our key line opens the stanza in a fresh way. "Their hearts are callous and unfeeling," the poet says of the arrogant, "but I delight in your law" (Psalm 119:70). The Hebrew is earthy and vivid. It says, roughly, that their heart has grown thick like fat, covered over and insensible. One way to read verses 70 and 71 together is as a diagnosis Paul Brand would have recognized at once. The proud men in this psalm have lost their nerve endings. Nothing reaches them anymore, so they wander without knowing the damage. The psalmist, meanwhile, has been hurt, and the hurt has kept him awake to God. His affliction functioned like a working nerve, the sharp signal that said, "Stop. You are drifting. Come home."

This is a tender truth, and it needs to be held gently. The psalmist does not claim that every sorrow is a punishment, and he never calls suffering pleasant. He speaks as a man looking back, and he speaks inside a stanza that has just declared, "You are good, and what you do is good" (Psalm 119:68). His confidence rests on the character of God, and from there he can see that even the painful season was held by good hands. The letter to the Hebrews says the same thing with honesty: "No discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it" (Hebrews 12:11).

Perhaps you are in a season that aches. It might be a diagnosis, a quiet loneliness, a business that is struggling, a child who will not call, or the sting of being misunderstood by people you tried to serve well. The temptation in seasons like these is to numb the ache as quickly as possible, with busyness, with scrolling late into the night, or with a hardness that decides it will simply stop caring. The psalmist offers a gentler path. He lets the ache bring him to God, and he turns his pain into a prayer for understanding: "Teach me knowledge and good judgment, for I trust your commands" (Psalm 119:66).

Brand's patients learned to sit down each evening and look carefully at their hands and feet, searching for any small wound they had not felt during the day. You might borrow that habit for your heart tonight. Before you sleep, sit quietly for a few minutes and ask the Lord what the present difficulty is guarding you from, and what it might be teaching you about his word. It can help to remember an older hard season, one you have already come through, and to name one thing you learned there that you would not trade away now. Then pray verse 68 aloud over the trouble in front of you, slowly enough to mean it.

The ache you carry today may be the very nerve that keeps your heart tender toward God. A heart that can still feel is a heart he can still reach, and a heart he can reach is a heart he can heal. The poet of Psalm 119 discovered that the hard road had led him to a treasure worth more than "thousands of pieces of silver and gold" (Psalm 119:72). By his grace, you will one day look back on this season and say with that same quiet gratitude, "It was good for me."

articles.title: Letters Written by Lamplight
articles.dek: A Chinese commander at war spent his nights writing advice home to his family. Centuries earlier, a Hebrew teacher wrote thirty sayings for his students, and he stopped to tell them exactly why.
articles.quote: Every good saying is meant to do one thing in the end: teach your heart to lean its whole weight on God.
articles.illustration: Zeng Guofan's family letters, Qing China
articles.body:
In the 1850s, while China was being torn apart by the Taiping Rebellion, a scholar-turned-commander named Zeng Guofan spent his evenings in army tents doing something that seemed far too small for a man at war. He wrote letters home. By lamplight, between reports of lost cities and hard-won battles, he wrote to his younger brothers and to his sons about ordinary things: rising early, keeping the household accounts honest, reading a few pages every day, treating servants with kindness, and living simply even as the family grew important. Over the course of his life he wrote well over a thousand of these letters.

After his death the letters were gathered and published as his Family Letters, and they have been read in Chinese homes for generations since. What moves historians most is what happened inside his own family. His son Zeng Jize taught himself English as a grown man and became one of China's early envoys to Britain, France, and Russia, where he negotiated patiently and honestly on his country's behalf. Later generations produced a long line of scholars and educators, and a great-granddaughter, Zeng Baosun, became a Christian, studied in London, and returned home to found a school for girls in Changsha. The father had been gone for decades, yet his words were still at work in the people he loved.

Any Filipino who grew up with a lola's bilin, or with a parent working abroad whose voice came home through long-distance calls and handwritten notes tucked inside a balikbayan box, understands Zeng Guofan. The things a parent says over and over, like "Mag-ingat ka" or "Huwag kang mangungutang," eventually become the voice a grown child hears when no one else is around. Words repeated in love have a way of outliving the one who spoke them.

Proverbs 22:17 opens with that same kind of voice. Up to this point, from 10:1 to 22:16, the book has been a collection of Solomon's short, two-line proverbs, each one complete in itself. At verse 17 the style changes. A teacher begins speaking directly to a student, in longer units, under a new heading: "the sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17). In 1923 the German Egyptologist Adolf Erman pointed out that this section closely resembles an Egyptian work called the Instruction of Amenemope, written by an official for his son and arranged in thirty chapters. That discovery helped explain a puzzling word in verse 20. Older English Bibles translated it "excellent things," but most scholars now read it as "thirty," and the NIV renders it "thirty sayings." Roughly thirty units of counsel follow, running through 24:22. Israel's teachers knew the wisdom of their neighbors and were willing to use a good form when they found one.

The Hebrew teacher, however, put something into that form that changes its whole purpose. Before he gives a single piece of advice, he pauses to tell his student why he is teaching at all.

"Pay attention and turn your ear to the sayings of the wise; apply your heart to what I teach, for it is pleasing when you keep them in your heart and have all of them ready on your lips. So that your trust may be in the LORD, I teach you today, even you." (Proverbs 22:17–19)

The Egyptian instruction aims mainly at producing a calm, self-controlled official who rises smoothly at court. The Hebrew sage borrows the shape and gives it a new heart: "So that your trust may be in the LORD" (Proverbs 22:19). The sayings that follow are intensely practical. Do not move an ancient boundary stone (22:28). Do not make friends with a hot-tempered person (22:24). "Do not wear yourself out to get rich; do not trust your own cleverness" (23:4). Each one is a small, concrete way of taking your weight off your own strength and placing it on God. One way to read this whole section is as thirty lessons in a single subject, which is trust. Every good saying is meant to do one thing in the end: teach your heart to lean its whole weight on God.

The words the teacher chooses for how wisdom should be kept are vivid. When the NIV says "keep them in your heart," the Hebrew literally says keep them "in your belly," using beten, a word for a person's innermost depths. Wisdom is meant to be taken all the way in, the way food is swallowed and becomes part of the body. Then he wants these sayings "ready on your lips," from the Hebrew root kun, which means to be set firm, established, prepared. The picture is of truth swallowed deep and then standing ready, so that when the moment of temptation or decision comes, the right word is already there. Zeng Guofan's sons did not open a book of letters every time they faced a choice. The letters had become part of them.

The teacher also makes it personal. "I teach you today, even you" (22:19). In Hebrew the phrase is emphatic, as if the teacher has stopped addressing a classroom and is now looking one student in the eye. God's wisdom was never meant to be general advice for humanity at large. It comes to you, today, by name.

Here the gospel opens up the passage. Sayings, however wise, cannot by themselves make a person trust. Israel had the finest wisdom in the ancient world and still wandered from God again and again. Many of us know the right proverbs and still worry, still grasp, still trust our own cleverness. The New Testament answers this by showing that God's wisdom finally arrived as a Person. Paul writes that we are "in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30), and that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). The trust Proverbs aims at finds its resting place in Jesus, who kept every saying perfectly and then gave his life for those who broke them. When you fail to live by what you know, the goal of the lesson still stands, and the way back to it is open: you trust him again, and you receive his grace again.

The passage closes with a picture worth carrying. The teacher is training his student "to be honest and to speak the truth, so that you bring back truthful reports to those you serve" (22:21). The Hebrew more literally says "to those who send you," which pictures the student as a messenger, someone entrusted with carrying word faithfully between people. It is a fitting image for Zeng Jize, who grew up on his father's letters and spent his career carrying honest reports between nations. It is also a fitting image for every believer. "We are therefore Christ's ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us" (2 Corinthians 5:20). Wisdom that has truly gone into the belly comes out as honesty, at the office, in the barkada group chat, and in the report you give your boss when the numbers are disappointing.

You can begin taking this wisdom in today. Choose one saying from Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22, write it on a card or as your phone's lock screen, and say it aloud each morning and each night this week until it is ready on your lips without effort. If there is someone younger in your life, a child, a pamangkin, or a new coworker, consider sending them one short message of bilin, and tell them the reason the old teacher gave: so that their trust may be in the Lord.

Zeng Guofan never knew how far his lamplit letters would travel, and you will not know how far your faithfulness travels either. The same God who spoke to one student "today, even you" is speaking to you this morning. Take his words in deeply, keep them close, and lean on him. He has proven, again and again, that he can bear your weight.
